terms: Maximum population an environment can sustainably support.
Shift from high birth and death rates to low rates as societies industrialise.
Area of productive land needed to sustain a person's consumption and absorb their waste.
Thomas Malthus (1798) argued population grows faster than food supply, causing crises.
Bar chart by age and sex; shape reveals demographic stage and future trends.
Faster use of non-renewables (minerals, fossil fuels) than they form or can be substituted.
Ratio of actual energy output to maximum possible output; ~25% for solar PV, ~40% for offshore wind.
Mirrors focus sunlight to heat fluid driving a turbine; molten-salt storage allows night-time generation.
Hydrogen produced by electrolysing water with renewable electricity; potential for hard-to-electrify sectors.
Output fluctuations from solar and wind; managed by storage, demand response and grid mix.
Levelised Cost of Energy: average cost per MWh over a plant's lifetime.
Stores energy by pumping water uphill, releases by letting it fall through turbines.
Diffuse pollution from many sources (urban run-off, agricultural fertiliser).
PM10 and PM2.5: airborne particles linked to respiratory and cardiovascular disease.
Toxic compounds resistant to degradation, e.g., DDT, PCBs; covered by Stockholm Convention (2001).
Pollution from a single identifiable location (factory pipe, oil spill).
Released directly into the environment, e.g., SO2 from coal combustion.
Formed by reaction of primary pollutants, e.g., tropospheric ozone, sulfuric acid.
A square frame of known area placed on the ground to count or estimate the abundance of plants or slow-moving animals within it.
Choosing sample locations by chance, for example using random coordinates, to avoid bias and make results representative of the area.
The extent to which a measurement gives consistent results if repeated, improved by taking repeat readings and calculating a mean.
Selecting a representative subset of an area or population to study, since it is rarely possible to measure every organism or location.
A line laid across a habitat along which samples are taken at intervals to study how species change along a gradient such as distance from a shore.
The extent to which a method actually measures what it claims to, depending on appropriate controls and accurate, relevant techniques.
The maximum population size of a species that an environment can support indefinitely given its available resources.
The area of land and water needed to supply a population's resources and absorb its waste, used to gauge environmental demand.
A resource such as coal, oil or natural gas that exists in finite amounts and is not replaced on a human timescale once used.
A resource such as solar, wind or sustainably managed timber that can be replenished naturally within a human timescale.
Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, especially in resource use.
Using resources such as fisheries or forests at a rate that allows them to regenerate, for example through quotas and replanting.
The variety of living organisms in an area, measured at the level of genes, species and ecosystems, and an indicator of ecological health.
The protection and careful management of habitats and species to maintain biodiversity, for example through nature reserves and breeding programmes.
A community of living organisms together with the non-living physical environment, interacting as a system through energy flow and nutrient cycling.
A network of interconnected food chains showing the feeding relationships and flow of energy between organisms in a community.
A species whose presence has a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem, so that its loss would dramatically change the community.
A feeding position in a food chain, such as producer, primary consumer or secondary consumer, through which energy passes.
Human alteration of natural fluxes (e.g., Haber process doubled global reactive N input).
Pathway by which a chemical element moves through biotic and abiotic compartments of Earth.
Slow, sedimentary cycle: weathering of rocks releases phosphate; runs through life and back to ocean sediments.
Compartment storing a quantity of an element, e.g., ocean carbon, soil nitrogen.
Average time an element spends in a reservoir = reservoir size / flux.
Includes volcanic outgassing, biological reduction (DMS) and atmospheric oxidation to sulfate aerosols.
Sequence of reactions producing/destroying stratospheric O₃ (Chapman 1930).
Measure of ozone column thickness; 1 DU = 0.01 mm at STP.
Triatomic oxygen; concentrated in stratosphere ~15–35 km altitude.
315–400 nm; weakly absorbed; ageing and tanning.
280–315 nm; absorbed by O₃; harmful to DNA.
λ < 280 nm; absorbed by O₂ to produce atomic oxygen.
Region with ≥1500 endemic plants and ≥70% primary vegetation loss; 36 globally.
Variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes within a region.
Variation of alleles within a population, underpinning adaptive capacity.
H' = -Σ(pᵢ ln pᵢ); higher values indicate higher diversity.
Dominance-weighted index D = Σ(n/N)²; lower values indicate higher diversity.
Variety and relative abundance of species; combines richness and evenness.
~870 Gt C, increasing ~5 Gt yr⁻¹ from fossil fuel emissions.
Reservoir absorbing more CO₂ than it emits (e.g., oceans, growing forests).
Reservoir emitting more CO₂ than it absorbs (e.g., volcanoes, deforestation).
~38 000 Gt C — largest active reservoir; absorbs ~25% of anthropogenic CO₂.
Mean time a carbon atom remains in a reservoir; atmosphere ~5 yr, deep ocean centuries.
Carbon dioxide equivalent; common unit converting all GHGs via GWP.
Emissions per unit output (e.g., kg CO₂e per kWh).
WRI/WBCSD standard for corporate carbon accounting since 2001.
Direct emissions from owned/controlled sources (fuel, fugitive).
Indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heat or cooling.
All other indirect emissions in the value chain (15 categories per GHG Protocol).
Methane; GWP ≈ 25 over 100 yr; sources include livestock, wetlands, gas leaks.
Cumulative radiative forcing of 1 kg of a gas relative to 1 kg CO₂ over 100 yr.
Re-radiation of infrared energy by atmospheric gases warming Earth's surface.
Hydrofluorocarbons; refrigerants with GWPs up to ~14 000.
Nitrous oxide; GWP ≈ 298; major source agricultural soils.
Net change in energy flux at the tropopause (W m⁻²) due to a perturbation.
Minimum Ne 50 to avoid inbreeding short-term, 500 long-term (Franklin/Soulé).
Total count of individuals; usually >> Ne.
Number of breeders contributing equally to next generation.
Random change in allele frequencies, stronger in small populations.
Proportion of heterozygous loci; measure of genetic diversity.
Reduced fitness due to homozygosity of deleterious recessives.
Description of existing environmental conditions before the project.
Systematic identification and evaluation of environmental impacts of proposed projects.
Environmental Impact Statement; the formal report submitted for decision.
1985 Directive (consolidated 2011/92/EU) requiring EIA across Member States.
Identification of key issues and study boundaries.
Decision whether EIA is required (mandatory list, threshold, case-by-case).
Vehicle exhaust device that reduces NOx, CO and unburnt HC using Pt-Pd-Rh.
Oxides of nitrogen (NO, NO₂) from combustion; precursors to ozone and acid rain.
Particulate matter <2.5 μm diameter, capable of alveolar penetration.
Sulphur oxides from fossil fuel burning; cause acidification of rain (pH <5.6).
Secondary pollutant formed by NOx + VOCs + sunlight; damages lungs and crops.
High birth and death rates; stable, low population (pre-industrial).
Death rate falls (sanitation, medicine); rapid population growth.
Birth rate falls (education, urbanisation); slowing growth.
Low birth and death rates; population stabilises.
Birth rate below death rate; population decline (e.g., Japan, Italy).
Average children per woman; replacement level ~2.1.
Topsoil; mixed mineral and organic matter; site of most biological activity.
Subsoil; accumulation of leached clays, iron and aluminium oxides.
Weathered parent material; less biological activity.
Sand-silt-clay classification (USDA); determines drainage and fertility.
Largest catch that can be sustained indefinitely; at N = K/2 under logistic growth.
Setting catch limits below MSY to allow for uncertainty (FAO 1995).
Addition of young fish to the exploitable population.
Relationship between spawning biomass and recruitment (Beverton-Holt, Ricker).
Annual catch limit set by managers; allocated as quotas.
